title: Scripts: tests, branching, loops & functions
about: The test command and conditions, if and case, for, while and until loops, functions and variable scope, reading and tracing small scripts, and spotting typical bugs.

questions.title: What [ is
questions.text: What is `[` in `if [ -f "$1" ]; then`?

options.t: A command (a synonym of `test`) that evaluates the expression up to the closing `]` and returns 0 or 1.
options.why: `if` only looks at its exit status.
It is an ordinary command, which is why it needs spaces around it.

questions.title: Spaces matter
questions.text: Which of these is a correct test?

options.why: Spaces after `[` and before `]`, and around `=`.
Without spaces, bash looks for a command called `["$a"`.
A single word, which is always true (non-empty string).
The final `]` must be a separate word: "missing `]`".

questions.title: Numeric or string operator
questions.text: Classify each test operator.

items.why: Greater than or equal, as integers.
The file exists and has a size above zero.

questions.title: File tests
questions.text: Match each test with what it checks.

pairs.r: The path exists, of any type
It exists and is a regular file
It exists and is a directory
It exists and is not empty
It exists and you may execute it
pairs.why: Checks the permission for the current user.

questions.title: String and number tests
questions.text: Match each expression with its meaning.

pairs.r: `s` is empty
`s` is not empty
The two strings differ
`n` is at least 10 as a number
`f` does not exist

questions.title: Numbers as text
questions.text: What does `[ 10 \> 9 ]` (comparing with `\>`) return?

options.t: False: it compares the strings `10` and `9` alphabetically, and `1` sorts before `9`.
An error because `>` is not allowed.
options.why: It is a valid string comparison.
There it is also a string comparison.

questions.title: Empty variable surprise
questions.text: `x=""` and then `[ $x = y ]` (no quotes). What happens?

options.t: The test becomes `[ = y ]`, which is a syntax error: "unary operator expected".
It is false, without any message.

questions.title: Unquoted -n
questions.text: With `v=""`, what does `[ -n $v ]` (unquoted) return?

options.t: True (status 0), because the test sees only `[ -n ]`, a single non-empty word.

options.why: Only with quotes is the empty string preserved.
A single word is a valid test.

questions.title: Integer expected
questions.text: What does `[ 10 -eq 10.0 ]` do?

options.t: It fails with "integer expression expected", because `test` only compares integers with `-eq`.
options.why: The shell has no floating point.

options.t: It returns true, since both numbers are equal.
It returns false without a message.
options.why: A message is printed and the status is 2.

questions.title: Combining conditions
questions.text: Which of these is the clearest way to require two conditions?

options.why: Two tests joined with the shell's `&&`.
`&&` is not allowed inside a single `[ ]`; use `-a` or two tests.

questions.title: Double brackets
questions.text: Which feature does `[[ ]]` have that `[ ]` lacks?

options.t: Pattern matching with `==` and regular expressions with `=~`, and no word splitting of unquoted variables.
options.why: It is a bash keyword, not a portable `sh` feature.

options.t: It works in every POSIX shell.
options.why: It is an extension of bash, ksh and zsh.

options.t: It is faster because it is a separate program.
options.why: It is part of the shell.

questions.title: Arithmetic condition
questions.text: Which condition compares integers with familiar operators such as `>`?

options.why: Double parentheses evaluate an arithmetic expression; status 0 when it is non-zero.
That redirects output into a file named `3`.
String comparison of the text `x` and `3`.

questions.title: Dangerous redirection
questions.text: What does `[ $a > $b ]` do by mistake?

options.t: It runs `[ $a ]` and writes its output (nothing) into a new file whose name is the value of `b`, creating a stray file.
It produces a syntax error only.

questions.title: Is it a directory
questions.text: Check that `$1` is a directory: `if [ {{0}} "$1" ]; then`
questions.note: `-d` tests for a directory, `-f` for a regular file, `-e` for any path.

wrong.why: That is true only for regular files.
True for anything that exists, including files.

questions.title: Not empty
questions.text: Check that a variable `name` holds some text: `if [ {{0}} "$name" ]; then`

wrong.why: True when the string is empty: the opposite.

questions.title: Exit status as a condition
questions.text: Which `if` uses the exit status of `grep` directly, with no output?

options.why: `-q` silences the output; only the status matters.
`[` would try to interpret `grep` as an operand.
That would try to *run* the output.

questions.title: Status when no branch runs
questions.text: What is `$?` after `if false; then echo hi; fi`?

options.why: When no branch is executed, the `if` statement itself succeeds.
That was the status of the condition.

questions.title: Anatomy of an if
questions.text: Put the keywords of a complete two-way `if` in order.

items.why: Introduces the commands run when the condition is true.
Introduces the commands for the other case.

questions.title: Missing separator
questions.text: What is wrong with `if [ -f "$f" ] then echo yes; fi` on one line?

options.t: `then` cannot be used on one line.

questions.title: elif
questions.text: What does `elif` do?

options.t: It gives another condition to test when the previous `if` condition was false, without nesting a new block.
options.why: Only the first true branch runs.

options.t: It runs when the `if` condition is true.

questions.title: Trace: elif
questions.text: What does `n=5; if [ $n -lt 3 ]; then echo A; elif [ $n -lt 10 ]; then echo B; else echo C; fi` print?

options.why: The first condition is false; the second is true, so its branch runs and the rest is skipped.

questions.title: Chain of and/or
questions.text: What does `true || echo A && echo B` print?

options.why: `||` and `&&` have equal precedence and run left to right: `true` succeeds so `echo A` is skipped, then the status 0 lets `&& echo B` run.
`||` skips its right side when the left succeeds.

questions.title: Ternary style
questions.text: Which one-liner prints `yes` when `x` is empty, and `no` otherwise?

options.why: Fine here, because `echo yes` succeeds; if the middle command could fail, `||` would run too.
Runs `echo no` whenever the chain reaches it: different logic.

questions.title: case purpose
questions.text: When is `case` a better choice than a chain of `if`/`elif`?

options.t: When one value (a variable) is compared with several patterns, such as commands, options or file-name shapes.
options.why: It reads more clearly and supports glob patterns.

options.t: When you need to compare numbers with `<` and `>`.
When the script has no variables.
options.why: It needs a value to match.

questions.title: case patterns
questions.text: Match each pattern with what it matches.

pairs.r: Any word that starts with `a`
A single digit
The word `y` or the word `yes`
Anything (used as the default)
A name ending in `.txt` or `.md`

questions.title: Trace: case
questions.text: What does `for x in apple 42 ""; do case "$x" in [0-9]*) echo -n "num ";; "") echo -n "empty ";; *) echo -n "word ";; esac; done` print?

options.why: `apple` fits only `*`, `42` starts with a digit, and the empty string matches `""`.
The order follows the loop: apple first.
The empty string matches the `""` pattern.

questions.title: Double semicolon
questions.text: What does `;;` do in a `case`?

options.t: It ends the commands of a branch; after it, the `case` finishes.
options.why: Without it the next pattern would be parsed as a command.

questions.title: Menu with case
questions.text: Complete the default branch that catches every other value: `case "$1" in start) echo go;; stop) echo halt;; {{0}}) echo usage;; esac`
questions.note: `*` matches anything, so it must be the last pattern.

wrong.why: That is the word "default" itself as a pattern, matching only the text `default`.

questions.title: Quoting in case
questions.text: Why is `case "$answer" in` written with the variable in quotes?

options.t: So that an empty value or one with spaces still forms a single word instead of breaking the syntax.

options.why: It works without them in many cases.
Quotes do not change case handling.

options.t: To stop the script at errors.

questions.title: The loop forms
questions.text: Match each loop with how it decides to continue.

pairs.r: Runs once for each word in the list
Repeats while the condition succeeds (status 0)
Repeats while the condition fails (status non-zero)
Runs once for each positional parameter

extras.why: Only with a condition that never changes.

questions.title: for with a glob
questions.text: `for f in *.txt; do ...; done` in a directory with no `.txt` files. What value does `f` take?

options.t: The literal text `*.txt`, once, because an unmatched glob stays as it is.

options.why: With default options it runs once.

options.t: The first file of the directory.

questions.title: seq and ranges
questions.text: Which loop header visits the numbers 1 to 10?

options.why: Both give the list; brace expansion works with literals only.

questions.title: Variable limit in braces
questions.text: Why does `n=5; for i in {1..$n}` not loop five times?

options.t: Brace expansion happens before variable expansion, so `{1..$n}` is not a valid range and stays literal; use `$(seq 1 $n)` or a C-style `for`.
Because `seq` is required in all loops.

questions.title: C-style loop
questions.text: Which form is the arithmetic `for` of bash?

options.why: Initialisation, condition and step, like in C.

questions.title: break and continue
questions.text: What is the difference between `break` and `continue`?

options.t: `break` leaves the loop completely; `continue` skips the rest of the current pass and starts the next one.
options.why: Both accept a number for nested loops.

questions.title: Trace: continue and break
questions.text: What does `for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do [ $i -eq 2 ] && continue; [ $i -eq 4 ] && break; echo -n "$i "; done` print?

options.why: 2 is skipped by `continue`; at 4 the loop ends, so 5 is never reached.
At 4 the loop ends before printing.

questions.title: Trace: nested break
questions.text: What does `for i in 1 2 3; do for j in 1 2 3; do [ $j -eq 2 ] && break; echo -n "$i$j "; done; done` print?

options.why: `break` leaves only the inner loop at `j=2`, then the outer loop goes on.
The outer loop runs three times.

questions.title: Trace: counter
questions.text: What does `n=0; for f in a b c; do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n` print?

questions.title: Trace: sum of evens
questions.text: What does `s=0; for i in 1 2 3 4; do if [ $((i%2)) -eq 0 ]; then s=$((s+i)); fi; done; echo $s` print?

options.why: Even numbers do pass the test.

questions.title: Trace: until
questions.text: What does `i=0; until [ $i -ge 3 ]; do i=$((i+1)); done; echo $i` print?

options.why: The loop repeats while the condition is false and stops when `i` reaches 3.
One more step happens when `i` is 2.
It stops as soon as the condition becomes true.

questions.title: Trace: decreasing
questions.text: What does `k=5; while [ $k -gt 0 ]; do k=$((k-2)); done; echo $k` print?

options.why: 5, 3, 1 pass the test; then 1 becomes -1 and the loop ends.

questions.title: Reading pairs
questions.text: What does `t=0; while read -r a b; do t=$((t+b)); done <<< $'x 1\ny 2\nz 3'; echo $t` print?

options.why: Each line gives a label and a number; the numbers are added.
That is the number of lines.

questions.title: Loop in a pipe
questions.text: `c=0; printf 'a\nb\n' | while read l; do c=$((c+1)); done; echo $c` prints `0`. Why?

options.t: The loop after the pipe runs in a subshell, so its changes to `c` are lost when it ends.
options.why: Redirect the file into the loop, or use process substitution.

questions.title: Count lines of each file
questions.text: Put the steps of a script that prints, for each argument, the number of lines in that file in order.

items.t: Check that at least one argument was given
Loop over the arguments with `for f in "$@"`
Inside the loop, test that `$f` is a readable file

questions.title: Defining and calling
questions.text: What does this script print? `hello() { echo "Hi $1"; }; hello Ana; hello`

options.why: The second call has no argument, so `$1` is empty.

options.t: `Hi Ana` and an error for the second call.
options.why: A missing argument is simply empty.
Each call has its own parameters.

options.t: Nothing, functions must be declared with `function`.

questions.title: Function parameters
questions.text: Inside a function, what do `$1` and `$#` refer to?

options.t: To the arguments of the function call, not to those of the script.
options.why: Functions have their own positional parameters while they run.

options.t: To the arguments of the script.
options.why: They are hidden while the function runs.

options.t: Nothing, functions take no arguments in bash.

questions.title: Return values
questions.text: How does a bash function give a result to its caller?

options.t: Through its exit status with `return n` (0 to 255), or by printing text that the caller captures with `$(...)`.
options.why: There is no return of arbitrary values.

options.t: By assigning to the function's name.

questions.title: Trace: return
questions.text: What do `f() { return 3; echo never; }; f; echo $?` print?

options.why: `return` leaves the function immediately, and its number becomes `$?`.

questions.title: Capturing output
questions.text: What does `add() { echo $(( $1 + $2 )); }; r=$(add 2 3); echo "r=$r"` print?

options.why: The function prints `5`, and the substitution captures it.
The output was captured, not lost.

questions.title: Global by default
questions.text: What does `x=1; f() { x=2; }; f; echo $x` print?

options.why: Variables are global in bash unless declared `local`.
Assigning inside a function is fine.

questions.title: Local
questions.text: What does `x=1; f() { local x=2; }; f; echo $x` print?

options.why: `local` limits the variable to the function and its callees.

questions.title: Exit in a function
questions.text: A function contains `exit 1` and is called normally. What happens?

options.t: The whole script ends with status 1.
options.why: Use `return 1` to leave only the function.

options.t: The shell prints a warning and continues.

questions.title: Functions and scripts
questions.text: Why is a function often a better tool than an alias inside a script?

options.t: A function can take parameters, contain several commands and logic, and works in non-interactive shells where aliases are not expanded.
Aliases cannot be used at all in bash.

options.why: They must be defined before use.

questions.title: Define before use
questions.text: A script calls `greet` on line 3 but defines `greet()` on line 10. What happens?

options.t: The call fails with "command not found", because the function is defined only when bash executes the definition.
options.why: Put function definitions before the code that calls them.

options.t: It works, since bash reads the whole file first.

questions.title: Pass all arguments
questions.text: A function should process every argument it is given, even ones with spaces. Which loop is right?

options.why: Preserves each argument as a single word.

questions.title: Recursion
questions.text: Which is true about recursive functions in bash?

options.t: A function can call itself, and each call has its own `local` variables; use `local` or results come out wrong.
Recursion is not allowed in bash.

questions.title: Trace the execution
questions.text: Which command runs a script printing each command before it executes?

options.why: Each line is shown with a `+` prefix.
That only checks the syntax without running.
That prints the lines as they are read, without expansions.
That stops at the first failing command.

questions.title: Bash debugging options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Check the syntax without running the commands
Print each command with its expanded values as it runs
Print each line as read, before expansion
Treat unset variables as errors
Exit when a command fails

extras.r: Run the script in the background

questions.title: Bug: loop over files with spaces
questions.text: A script has `for f in $(ls); do rm "$f"; done`. What is the main problem?

options.t: `$(ls)` is split on spaces, so a file called `my notes.txt` becomes two words (`my` and `notes.txt`), and the wrong files are addressed.
options.why: Use `for f in *; do` which keeps names intact.

options.t: `ls` cannot be used in a loop.
options.why: It can, but it is fragile.

questions.title: Bug: assignment with spaces
questions.text: What is wrong with `COUNT = 0` at the top of a script?

options.t: Spaces around `=` make bash run a command named `COUNT`; the assignment must be `COUNT=0`.

questions.title: Bug: comparing numbers with =
questions.text: A script says `if [ $a = 10 ]` to compare numbers. When can that give a surprising result?

options.t: `=` compares strings, so `10` and `010` or `10 ` with spaces are different although numerically equal; use `-eq` for numbers.
options.why: Also, an empty `a` breaks the syntax unless quoted.

questions.title: Bug: rm with an empty variable
questions.text: What is the danger in `rm -rf $DIR/*` when `DIR` is empty or unset?

options.t: It expands to `rm -rf /*`, which tries to delete everything the user is allowed to.
options.why: Check the variable first and quote it: `[ -n "$DIR" ] && rm -rf "$DIR"/*`.

options.t: Nothing, it deletes nothing because `DIR` is empty.
It prints an error and stops.

options.why: `/*` does not match hidden files, but includes all other top-level entries.

questions.title: Bug: missing shebang target
questions.text: A script starts with `#!/bin/bsh` (typo). What happens when it is run with `./script.sh`?

options.t: "bad interpreter: No such file or directory", because the kernel cannot find the interpreter.
options.why: Also seen when the file has Windows line endings (`/bin/bash\r`).

options.t: Bash runs it anyway and ignores the typo.
It asks which interpreter to use.

questions.title: Bug: pipe in a loop and variable
questions.text: A script counts matches with `grep x file | while read l; do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n` and prints nothing useful. Why?

options.t: The loop runs in a subshell because of the pipe, so `n` in the parent is unchanged.
options.why: Use `n=$(grep -c x file)` or redirect the file into the loop.

questions.title: Bug: test on the wrong thing
questions.text: A script wants to check that `$1` is a non-empty regular file but writes `if [ -f $1 ]`. What is the flaw beyond the missing size check?

options.t: Unquoted `$1` breaks with names containing spaces or with an empty value (becoming `[ -f ]`, which is true); and `-f` does not check the size (`-s` does).
options.why: Quote, and use `-s` if emptiness matters.

questions.title: Bug: return value misuse
questions.text: A function ends with `return $result` where `result` holds the text `done`. What happens?

options.t: `return` complains: "numeric argument required"; it accepts only numbers, so print the text and capture it instead.

questions.title: Bug: wrong redirection in a check
questions.text: What is wrong with `if [ -f file.txt ] > /dev/null; then`?

options.t: Nothing harmful, but useless: `[` prints nothing, so there is no output to discard; errors would go to stderr anyway.
options.why: Redirecting output of a test is noise.

options.t: It makes the test always false.

questions.title: Order of checks
questions.text: Which order makes a robust script start?

options.t: Check arguments, then check that files or directories exist, then do the work, reporting errors to stderr and using distinct exit codes.
Do the work first and check afterwards.
Ignore errors to keep the script short.
options.why: Silent failures are hard to debug.

options.t: Always ask the user with `read` instead of using arguments.

questions.title: Tracing a pipeline
questions.text: What do `x=3; y=4; echo $((x**2 + y**2))` and `echo "$x + $y = $((x+y))"` print?

options.why: `**` is exponentiation; the text is printed and the last part is arithmetic.
`**` is the power operator, not multiplication.
The second command prints the whole string.
